## Paper

## Abstract

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are among the most persistent and challenging environmental pollutants. Compared with conventional oxidative or homogeneous reduction processes, electrochemical and photoelectrochemical reduction (ER and PER) offer reagent-free routes for PFAS destruction but remain limited by poor PFAS removal and sluggish defluorination under cathodic conditions. Here, we report a Pd-decorated TiO2 cathode that enables highly efficient photoelectrochemical degradation of perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) under ambient conditions. Operando spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism in which cathodic potentials promote PFAS adsorption on TiO2, while UV-excited Pd sites generate hot electrons that directly drive C–F bond cleavage or form hydrated electrons for indirect reduction. This dual-electron pathway leads to rapid and deep defluorination, outperforming previously reported ER and PER systems even in complex matrices such as reverse osmosis concentrate (ROC) and aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF)-impacted water. The study further demonstrates scalable single-chamber reactor designs and mesh-type cathodes, advancing the practical implementation of photoelectrochemical PFAS destruction technologies.

---

## Introduction

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemicals that have been widely used since the 1940s due to their desirable chemical properties. However, they pose a significant threat to the environment because of their toxicity and persistence.1,2 Oxidative destruction processes, such as the hydrothermal treatment3,4 and electrochemical oxidation (EO),5,6 have been extensively investigated. Despite their effectiveness, these approaches often require elevated temperatures and pressures or form harmful byproducts. Reductive defluorination offers an alternative treatment paradigm capable of achieving comparable effectiveness under mild conditions while minimizing or eliminating the formation of oxyanion byproducts.7

Homogeneous photochemical reductive treatment, such as UV activation of sulfite (UV/S), generates hydrated electrons (e-aq) to achieve broad-spectrum reactivity toward various PFAS.8 However, there remains a critical need for catalytic systems capable of continuously generating reductants without the need for chemical supply. For chemical-free treatment, particulate photocatalysts such as silicon carbide and boron nitride were employed to degrade perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) under UV254 nm irradiation.9,10 However, these catalytic systems have not been demonstrated to effectively degrade the more recalcitrant perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) unless more energy-intensive vacuum UV185 nm is irradiated.11

While the EO of PFAS on the anode has been extensively investigated, cathodic PFAS degradation remains a fundamental challenge. The research community has long sought breakthroughs in the electrochemical reduction (ER) or photoelectrochemical reduction (PER) pathways. Compared with the EO, far fewer investigations have been dedicated to this area. To date, reactive cathode materials, including carbon nanotubes modified by cationic surfactants,12–14 noble metals (Au and Pt),15,16 and diamond17 (summarized in Supplementary Table 1) have been explored. These studies revealed several fundamental challenges. It is widely recognized that the negatively charged PFAS molecules are typically repelled from the cathode.18,19 For example, a study clearly showed a three-order-of-magnitude drop in the PFOA partition coefficient between the aqueous phase and the Au surface when a negative potential was applied.15 Noticeable cathodic PFOS adsorption has previously been observed only on carbon nanotubes functionalized with cationic surfactants, where electrostatic attraction between the anionic PFOS headgroups and positively charged surfactant layers occurs.12 Even with successful PFAS adsorption on the cathode, achieving reductive defluorination is challenging. Under cathodic potential, water reduction readily occurs as a competing reaction, generating hydrogen and consuming a substantial portion of the electrons that could otherwise drive PFAS defluorination. This process may decrease the overall current efficiency but also hinders PFAS adsorption by occupying surface-active sites. To date, there exist only a few instances of confirmed PER removal of PFOS and limited defluorination in laboratory-prepared water.12,13 Key knowledge gaps remain, including the need for insights and solutions for the selective adsorption and reduction of perfluoroalkane sulfonic acids (PFSAs) and other PFAS in complex real-world water matrices, the optimal design of cathodes and reactors, and comprehensive assessments and demonstrations of scalability for practical applications.

Our central hypothesis is that a highly efficient PER cathode must contain reactive centers capable of generating strongly reducing species. Prior studies have shown that UV irradiation can excite 4d-band electrons in Pd through interband transitions, producing energetic hot electrons (e-hot).20 Based on our preliminary electronic structure analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1), the transient energies of these e-hot on Pd correspond to an effective reduction potential of approximately -4.2 V versus normal hydrogen electrode (VNHE), which is substantially more negative than the -2 V threshold required for PFOS reduction.7 Therefore, Pd is expected to function as the defluorination-active center. However, because PFAS adsorption is intrinsically challenging under cathodic polarization, we hypothesize that Pd must be integrated with an appropriate substrate to enable strong PFAS adsorption and efficient electron transfer.

This study marks a significant breakthrough in PER and ER treatment for PFAS. We report the scalable and facile synthesis of a Pd-decorated TiO2 cathode with dual functionality for PFAS adsorption and defluorination. Using a combination of operando characterization and theoretical calculations, we reveal a mechanism whereby cathodic current enhances PFAS adsorption on TiO2. The adsorbed PFAS is subsequently defluorinated either directly by e-hot generated at UV-excited Pd sites or indirectly via e-aq derived from these e-hot. The PER process demonstrates exceptional efficacy in degrading PFOS, even in the presence of complex, competitive matrices. Moving beyond proof-of-concept, we designed and validated a scalable PER system for the effective treatment of PFAS mixtures in membrane concentrates and simulated firefighting equipment cleaning solutions.

---

## Results

Catalyst Design, Electrode Synthesis and Characterization
The proposed catalyst used in ER and PER systems consists of Pd nanoparticles (NPs) embedded in TiO2 matrices. As will be revealed later, TiO2 not only acts as a support to disperse and immobilize Pd NPs but is a prerequisite for PFAS adsorption through a novel cathodic mechanism. The Pd NPs are designed as active sites to generate e-hot for PFAS defluorination. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 and the associated extended discussion, we estimated the energy level of these e-hot on Pd to be approximately -4.2 V. The application of a cathodic potential can shift the Fermi level of Pd to a more negative value, thereby endowing the e-hot with even greater reductive power to facilitate reductive defluorination of PFAS (Supplementary Fig. 1).

We prepared self-standing electrodes composed of a Ti metal substrate and a Pd-TiO2 catalyst layer. The electrodes were fabricated by coating a Ti metal plate with sol-gels of metal-citrate complexes, followed by calcination in air and subsequent electrochemical reduction in electrolytes. The calcination of Ti-citrate sol-gel yielded anatase TiO2, as revealed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (Fig. 1a). The calcination of mixed Ti- and Pd-citrate sol-gel produced palladium oxide (PdO)-doped TiO2 as indicated by the PdO peaks in XRD and the Pd2+feature in X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Fig. 1b). Upon applying 15 mA cm-2 cathodic current for 10 min in a 100 mM Na2SO4 electrolyte, Pd was electrochemically reduced to Pd0 (Fig. 1b). XRD analysis revealed well-defined Pd0 crystallinity with a dominant Pd (111) facet and the anatase TiO2 with a dominant TiO2 (101) facet. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM; Fig. 1c) imaging confirmed the presence of Pd nanoparticles (NPs) embedded in the TiO2 matrix, and the electron diffraction pattern confirmed the presence of Pd (111) and Pd (200) facets. The average diameter of Pd NPs is 11.6 nm.

The molar ratio of Pd/Ti in Pd-TiO2 was controlled by modifying the Pd/Ti ratio in sol-gel precursors. For example, Fig. 1d shows a scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of Pd-TiO2 with a pre-designed Pd/Ti molar ratio of 0.2 in the sol-gel. Energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) mapping measured a 0.22 Pd/Ti ratio, which is close to the target value. Cross-sectional SEM-EDS mapping of the Pd-TiO2 plate cathode (Pd/Ti = 0.2) reveals a Pd signal corresponding to a coating thickness of about 2-3 μm (Fig. 1e). Note that the Ti substrate and the Pd-TiO2 layer contribute to the Ti emission, the thickness cannot be accurately derived from the Ti signal. Lastly, the Pd-TiO2 cathode surface is hydrophilic, as evidenced by the spreading of a water droplet and the small contact angle (Fig. 1f). This observation implies that PFAS adsorption on Pd-TiO2 via hydrophobic interactions is unlikely.

Cathodic defluorination of PFOS
We first investigated the cathodic removal of PFAS via ER and PER using a dual-chamber electrolytic cell (Fig. 2a). A proton exchange membrane (Nafion 117) separated the anodic water oxidation reaction from the cathodic PFAS treatment. All electrode geometric areas reported in the manuscript refer to the double-sided projected area submerged in the electrolyte. Either the plate-type TiO2 or the Pd-TiO2 cathode (16 cm2) was placed in the cathodic chamber, which contained 100 mL of Na2SO4 catholyte spiked with PFOS (10 µM). A dimensionally stable iridium tantalum oxide anode (Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox; 16 cm2) served as the counter electrode. The anolyte was 100 mL of 100 mM H2SO4. To introduce UV254 nm irradiation, a quartz jacketed 18-W low-pressure Hg lamp (Pen-Ray; Analytik Jena) was inserted into the catholyte, positioned 0.5 cm from the cathode. During the treatment, catholyte samples were collected for PFOS analysis, as detailed in the Method section. Defluorination efficiency (DeF) was calculated as the percentage of recovered fluoride relative to the total amount of fluorine in the original PFOS.

We conducted a series of control tests (24 h) to rule out possible PFOS removal pathways that are unrelated to ER and PER reactions (Supplementary Fig. 2). We then investigated the ER treatment of PFOS. As an n-type semiconductor, TiO2 exhibits metallic conductivity under cathodic potentials.21,22 Cyclic voltammetry profiles (Supplementary Fig. 3) indicate an onset potential of hydrogen evolution at -1 and -0.5 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE) for TiO2 and Pd-TiO2, respectively. While open circuit TiO2 did not adsorb PFOS (Supplementary Fig. 2a), we surprisingly observed approximately 20% PFOS removal on TiO2 at -15 mA cm-2 after 8 h (Fig. 2b). This PFOS removal was not accompanied by defluorination, as no F- was detected (Fig. 2c). Therefore, we attribute PFOS removal by the TiO2 cathode to adsorption under cathodic potentials. This finding is unexpected because PFOS is an anion in solution and should be repelled by the negatively charged cathode. Thus, an uncovered mechanism other than the common electrostatic attraction or hydrophobic interactions must be responsible for PFOS adsorption.

Palladium doping further enhances the ER removal of PFOS After 8 hours of applied cathodic current, 55% of PFOS was removed (Fig. 2b). Methanol extraction of the used Pd-TiO2 cathode recovered 25% of PFOS, indicating that at least 25% of the original PFOS was removed through non-reactive adsorption. To evaluate SO42- formation resulting from desulfonation, the ER treatment was performed in NaClO4 catholyte, and the yield of SO42- was observed (Supplementary Fig. 4a). We estimate that approximately 28% of PFOS underwent C–S bond cleavage. When combined with the ~25% assigned to non-reactive adsorption, a total of 53% of PFOS is accounted for by adsorption-related pathways. This value closely matches the 55% PFOS removal determined from the decrease in aqueous-phase PFOS concentration (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 4b). Since no defluorination was detected in ER mode (Fig. 2c), we posit that the remaining perfluoroalkyl tails were adsorbed on the Pd-TiO2 surface after C–S bond cleavage. Further, we found no PFOS release upon discontinuation of the cathodic current (Supplementary Fig. 5), suggesting that while the cathodic current initiated the adsorption, it did not require sustained charges.

Under UV254 nm irradiation and cathodic currents (PER mode), we observed substantial PFOS removal and defluorination on the Pd-TiO2 cathode (Fig. 2b and c). Methanol extraction of the spent cathode did not detect any adsorbed PFOS, indicating that removal was due to degradation rather than adsorption. A performance comparison of Pd-TiO2 electrodes with Pd/Ti molar ratios ranging from 0.1 to 0.8 in PER mode (Supplementary Fig. 6) demonstrated that a 0.2 Pd/Ti ratio achieved the fastest PFOS removal and the highest DeF. Therefore, the Pd-TiO2 cathode with a 0.2 Pd/Ti ratio was selected for use in all subsequent experiments. The increase of cathodic current (5-20 mA cm-2) promotes PFOS removal in PER mode (Supplementary Fig. 7). A current density of 15 mA cm-2 was identified as the optimal condition, balancing fast PFOS removal kinetics and low electric energy consumption.

The substantial defluorination of PFOS by Pd-TiO2 under PER mode suggests that this removal was primarily due to destruction. The 37% DeF represents one of the highest values reported to date for ER and PER systems (Supplementary Table 1).12,13 In addition to defluorination, we observed 90% desulfonation (Supplementary Fig. 4a). The remaining 10% gap in sulfur balance is likely due to the formation of products that retain the sulfonate structure, as will be discussed in subsequent sections. Throughout the PER treatment, the catholyte pH was not actively controlled. To prevent pH elevation in the catholyte, an effect commonly observed when using a neutral salt solution as the anolyte,23 we employed 100 mM H2SO4 as the anolyte. In this configuration, excess protons migrated through the membrane, generating a proton flux that surpassed the rate of consumption via cathodic hydrogen evolution. As a result, the catholyte pH decreased from approximately 6 to 3 within the first two hours and then stabilized (Supplementary Fig. 8). Nevertheless, the acidification had little influence on PFOS removal and defluorination, as comparable performance was observed when phosphate buffer was used as the catholyte to maintain a constant pH of 7 throughout the PER treatment (Supplementary Fig. 8). The acidification is undesirable for practical water treatment applications, a single-chamber reactor design is introduced in subsequent sections to mitigate this issue.

Furthermore, we prepared Pd-loaded carbon cloth (Pd/CC), in which TiO2 was replaced by carbon cloth as the substrate, and evaluated its performance in the PER treatment of PFOS. The Pd/CC electrode exhibited PFOS removal under open-circuit conditions owing to adsorption by the CC substrate. However, it did not facilitate further PFOS removal or defluorination under PER operation (Supplementary Fig. 9). These results indicate that Pd NPs alone are insufficient to drive PFOS adsorption or reductive destruction, and that the TiO2 support plays an essential role in enabling PER activity.

Mechanisms of Promoted PFOS Adsorption Under Cathodic Potentials.
The used Pd-TiO2 cathode after ERC was characterized by attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR). Compared with the fresh Pd-TiO2 before the reaction with its essentially complete transmission, the used cathode has broad dips at 1000-1400 cm-1 and 600-800 cm-1 (Fig. 3a). These features are attributed to -CF2- (1150 cm-1 and 1250 cm-1), -CF3 (1200 cm-1), and -S=O (1200 and 650 cm-1).24–26 The results of ex-situ FTIR support the conjecture of retained PFOS and other polyfluorinated structures on the Pd-TiO2 surface.

We conducted operando FTIR measurements of Pd-TiO2 during the ER reaction to probe the adsorption mechanism (Fig. 3b and c). The time-zero FTIR reference at open circuit showed a broad peak between 1000-1400 cm-1, corresponding to -CF2- and -CF3 bond vibration in solution. The application of cathodic current led to the decrease of transmittance (i.e., enhanced IR absorbance) for -CF3 at 1200 cm-1 and -CF2- at 1150 cm-1, indicating the enrichment of PFOS on the cathode surface under the cathodic current. Upward peaks in the 1200-1400 cm⁻¹ range were observed, which corresponds to the inhibition of specific -CF2- bond vibrations. Such inhibition would lead to reduced IR light absorption and increased transmittance compared to the time-zero reference (without applied current). This result strongly suggests that cathodic adsorption inhibited the vibration of some C-F bonds on the side of the fluoroalkane chain, suggesting a co-planar adsorption configuration. Similar FTIR patterns were consistently observed across various cathodic current densities and potentials (Supplementary Fig. 10), confirming that PFOS adsorption is enhanced under cathodic polarization.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations provide detailed thermodynamic evidence and mechanistic insight into the cathodic adsorption mechanism. Periodic boundary condition DFT calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) to investigate the interactions between PFOS and Pd [111] and TiO2 [101] surfaces. These surface terminations were chosen because they are the experimentally dominant facets, as demonstrated by XRD, and are the thermodynamically expected surfaces. Given that the experimental catholyte pH of 3 (Supplementary Fig. 8), PFOS was modeled in its deprotonated state using a Hess cycle, referenced to the gas-phase PFOS and accounting for experimental solvation and deprotonation energies. The experimental cathodic potential of -0.5 V vs NHE was accounted for by placing an electron in the conduction band of TiO2 or, in the case of Pd, using the computational hydrogen electrode. Solvation effects were included using a hybrid method with an explicit H2O monolayer on the slab and implicit solvation filling the vacuum space between the slab and its periodic image, following the method of our previous work.27

The process of PFOS adsorption under cathodic current first requires the desorption of surface water molecules that form a hydrated layer on TiO2 and Pd. As shown in Fig. 4a, water binds moderately to the titanium sites on the TiO2 [101] surface, with desorption energies of 0.12 eV for one and 0.49 eV for two water molecules, but binds more strongly to Pd, requiring 0.46 eV and 0.73 eV, respectively.

Only after the water molecules are displaced does PFOS adsorption become possible. The DFT calculations predict that PFOS adsorbs on TiO2 with an exothermic binding energy of -3.81 eV (excluding water removal) and -3.69 eV after accounting for the water desorption energy penalty. The driving force for this water-replacement step arises from the stronger electrostatic and coordination interactions between the sulfonate oxygens of PFOS and the exposed Ti4+ sites, which compensate for the small energy penalty of removing surface water. Conversely, on Pd, the adsorption energy is -1.36 eV before and -0.74 eV after water removal, indicating that PFOS adsorption is unlikely on cathodic Pd, and therefore, that adsorption is restricted to TiO2 under cathodic conditions (-0.5 V vs NHE, pH 3). The large energy penalty for displacing water on Pd is attributed to the strong H-bonding network of the hexagonally arranged H2O monolayer. This theoretical prediction agrees well with experimental observations that when Pd is loaded on carbon cloth (Pd/CC) in the absence of TiO2, the Pd centers do not contribute to PFOS removal (Supplementary Fig. 9).

Supplementary Fig. 11a shows two possible adsorption configurations on TiO2. In the monodentate mode, PFOS replaces one water molecule; in the bidentate mode, it replaces two, with adsorption energies differing by 0.6 eV, making the monodentate configuration thermodynamically more favorable. The PFOS molecule adopts a coplanar geometry, where the perfluoroalkyl tail lies parallel to the surface (Fig. 4b), which is in agreement with our operando FTIR measurements. A similar geometry is observed for adsorption on Pd (Fig. 4c), although this pathway is not energetically favorable. It is important to note that the DFT-predicted coplanar adsorption of PFOS represents the lowest-energy configuration among multiple simulated geometries and does not imply hydrophobic interactions between the perfluoroalkyl tail and the TiO2 or Pd surface or hydrophobic repulsion of the PFOS from solution. The DFT simulations used the polarizable continuum model (PCM) implicit solvation to represent the water phase, and PCM methods do not model the configurational fluctuations and the disruption of H-bonding networks that lower the entropy of the solvated system and drive hydrophobic exosolvation.28,29 Similar coplanar adsorption has been reported for PFOA on gold surfaces,15 which is known to be hydrophilic,30 illustrating that adsorption geometry alone should not be interpreted as evidence of hydrophobic interactions.

Bader charge analysis (Supplementary Table 2) provides insight into the electronic origin of this co-planar adsorption preference. The surface titanium cations carry a charge of +2.04 e-, corresponding to a formal +4 oxidation state, while surface oxygens exhibit partial negative Bader charges (-1.35 to -1.40 e-), corresponding to a formal charge of -2. As shown in Supplementary Table 3, upon desorption of one surface water molecule, the exposed Ti atom gains 0.23 e-, and neighboring O atoms lose 0.15 e⁻, creating an electron-deficient region that strongly attracts the negatively charged sulfonate oxygen. During PFOS adsorption, about 0.15 e- is transferred from PFOS into the TiO2 lattice, distributing across the bonding Ti atoms and the partially empty surface and subsurface Ti-O states (Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 11b). These charge-transfer and coordination effects explain why Ti4+/Ti3+ centers act as the primary adsorption sites.

Desulfonation and Defluorination Mechanisms
As demonstrated above, PFOS adsorption only requires TiO2 filled with conduction band electrons, but defluorination occurs only in the presence of both Pd and UV irradiation. Our estimation based on band structure and photon energy suggests that UV excitation of Pd generates highly reductive e-hot (Supplementary Fig. 1). These energetic e-hot may react directly with adsorbed PFAS on the catalyst surface. We relied on multiple e-aq quenchers to prove that e-aq are critical in the PER reaction. The addition of SeO42- (5-10 mM; rate constant with e-aq: k = 1.1×109 M-1 s-1)31 and Cd2+ (5-10 mM; k = 4.8×1010 M-1 s-1)31 noticeably inhibited the PFOS removal and defluorination (Supplementary Fig. 12). Perchlorate (ClO4-) and chlorate (ClO3-) are inert to ER. Thus, they cannot be reduced by the Pd-TiO2 cathode under ER mode. However, these oxyanions are moderately reactive toward e-aq,32 and their removal under PER mode (Supplementary Fig. 13) confirms the existence of e-aq.

We further introduce dissolved oxygen via air purging into the PER system. The removal of PFOS was slowed due to the scavenging of e-aq by dissolved oxygen at 4.1 mg L-1 (Supplementary Fig. 14).33 However, PFOS removal and defluorination by PER continued effectively. A critical observation was that the presence of Cd2+ and SeO42- almost completely halted defluorination, whereas defluorination still occurred in the presence of dissolved oxygen. Since the cathodic electrodeposition of Cd2+ to Cd0 and SeO42- to Se0 has been well documented,34,35 and EDS mapping shows clear Cd and Se signals on the Pd-TiO2 cathode surface after reaction (Supplementary Fig. 12), it is reasonable to infer that the deposited Cd and Se poison Pd active sites responsible for defluorination.

The use of dissolved oxygen as a quencher should not alter the surface properties of Pd-TiO2. Kinetic analysis revealed that 4.1 mg L-1 dissolved oxygen could quench over 99% of the e-aq in the aqueous phase (Supplementary Fig. 14). Therefore, the observed defluorination of PFOS in the presence of dissolved oxygen must be attributed to e-hot residing on the Pd-TiO2 surface. By comparing the PFOS removal kinetics with and without dissolved oxygen, we estimated that e-aq and e-hot contributed 63% and 37% to PFOS removal, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 14).

The ability of the PER system to sustain PFOS degradation in the presence of oxygen overcomes a key limitation of conventional homogeneous advanced reductive processes, which require strictly oxygen-deficient environments.33,36 This unique feature enhances the versatility of PER and facilitates scale-up using membrane-less reactor configurations that are simpler and more practical than traditional dual-chamber designs, as discussed in later sections.

The reaction energy profiles of intermediates along various possible PFOS degradation pathways on Pd-TiO2 calculated by DFT are illustrated in Fig. 4d. The interaction of PFOS with the Pd-TiO2 surface is visualized in Fig. 4e. As discussed above, PFOS adsorption on TiO2 (state 2TiO2) is significantly more exothermic than on Pd (state 2Pd), and therefore thermodynamically more favorable. We further calculated various possible binding configurations of perfluoroalkyl tail groups (state 3) and sulfonate head group (state 5) interacting with TiO2 and Pd. The results show that the tail group on Pd (3Pd) and the head group on TiO2 (3TiO2) is the most thermodynamically favorable scenario.

Bader charge analysis (Supplementary Table 4) provides rationales for this finding. When the C-S bond breaks on TiO2, approximately 0.48 e⁻ is transferred from the surface to the fluorinated tail, leaving the surface Ti and O atoms electron-deficient by about 0.33 e⁻. When the tail subsequently migrates to a Pd site, TiO2 regains those 0.33 e⁻, while Pd donates electrons to the perfluoroalkyl group instead. On Pd, the tail receives an even greater charge transfer (0.62 e⁻) due to the abundance of Pd d electrons that stabilize the fragment. In contrast, the sulfonate moiety is stabilized on TiO2 after the C–S bond cleavage, gaining approximately 0.54 e⁻ from the surface once the electron-withdrawing tail departs. If the sulfonate group were to transfer from TiO2 to Pd, it would lose this electron density to Pd, making the process energetically unfavorable.

The DFT results rationalize the experimental observation that Pd-TiO2 outperforms bare TiO2 in PFOS adsorption and defluorination (Fig. 2b). This enhanced performance arises because the Pd-TiO2 interface facilitates C-S bond cleavage and tail-group migration to Pd, thereby regenerating TiO2 sites for continued PFOS adsorption and reaction while also preventing the reverse C-S bond formation reaction. This mechanism also explains why, under ER mode, Pd–TiO2 exhibits both reactive and non-reactive adsorption (Supplementary Fig. 4b). Once the Pd surface becomes fully covered by perfluoroalkyl tail groups, it can no longer sustain the C-S bond cleavage required for reactive adsorption. In contrast, under PER mode, the UV-excited Pd sites promote continuous tail-group destruction, enabling cyclic regeneration of adsorption and degradation sites at the Pd–TiO2 interface.

After the C-S scission, the perfluorooctyl chain could be subjected to C-F scission or chain-shortening by C-C scission (intermediates “4a-b” in Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 15). However, these steps are predicted to be highly endothermic, which is in agreement with the experimental results that Pd-TiO2 in ER mode alone did not lead to defluorination (Fig. 2c). The C-F scission may only be facilitated by energetic electrons (e-aq or e-hot). Biswas et al. have shown that the barrier to break the C-F bond of PFOS by e-aq was only about 0.08 eV (8.16 kJ mol-1).37 We suggest, therefore, that the C-F bond scission of the perfluoroalkyl tail is initiated by energetic electrons on Pd sites under the PER mode. Biswas et al. also found that the defluorination by e-aq was limited by the diffusion of the e-aq to the PFOS group.37 In our system, the perfluoroalkyl tail is directly bound to the Pd sites, placing it in proximity to the generated e-aq and e-hot. Consequently, we propose that C-F bond scission occurs through the action of photoexcited electrons. This mechanism accounts for the observed defluorination of PFOS exclusively on Pd-TiO2 under PER conditions.

These insights further underscore the critical role of cathodic adsorption in the PER system. Without cathodic current, PFOS removal was not observed on Pd-TiO2 under UV irradiation (Fig. S2b). The implications are two-fold: first, photoexcited TiO2 alone does not sustain PFOS adsorption, as photogenerated electrons rapidly migrate to Pd sites via Schottky contact,21 which, unlike TiO2, are unfavorable for PFOS adsorption, as discussed above. Second, without the cathodic adsorption of PFOS and C-S cleavage on TiO2 as the initial step, even if e-hot are generated on Pd sites, these excited electrons remain within the solid state and will rapidly relax to the Fermi level of Pd within femtoseconds to picoseconds.38,39

In PER mode, several synergistic effects are involved. Specifically, cathodic adsorption of PFOS and C-S bond cleavage on TiO2, along with the transfer of perfluoroalkyl groups to Pd, facilitate intimate contact between the perfluoroalkyl group and highly reducing e-hot on Pd. Meanwhile, the cathodic potential elevates the energy of e-hot on Pd beyond the vacuum level (Supplementary Fig. 1c), enabling electron emission from the solid phase into the aqueous phase. This process generates e-aq at the electrode-solution interface to react with adsorbed PFOS and Pd immobilized perfluoroalkyl group.40 Therefore, e-hot and e-aq jointly contribute as active reductive species responsible for PFOS defluorination.

We employed high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with either a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (HPLC-MS/MS) or quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (HPLC-Q-ToF-MS) to analyze the transformation products (TPs) of PFOS during the PER treatment. Our targeted analyte list included 30 C1-C10 PFAS (Supplementary Table 5), and our suspect screening protocol was capable of detecting H/F exchange products across various chain lengths.5 Despite the comprehensive approach, only one H/F exchange product retaining the sulfonate group was identified, with an estimated concentration of ~0.8 μM (Supplementary Fig. 16). This accounted for approximately 8% of the remaining gap sulfur mass balance (Supplementary Fig. 4a), thereby closing the overall sulfur balance. The formation of H/F exchange TPs strongly supports an electron-mediated hydrodefluorination pathway,41 driven by both e-aq and e-hot. PFOA was the only shorter-chain perfluorinated compound detected, and it was further degraded at the end of the reaction. The transient appearance of PFOA supports a chain-shortening degradation pathway, which could stem from the reaction between perfluoroalkyl groups and both e-aq and e-hot.

Environmental Applications and Scale Up
The presence of UV-absorbing natural organic matter (NOM), introduced into the catholyte at concentrations of 10-100 mg L-1 as total organic carbon (TOC), slowed the PER reaction kinetics. Nevertheless, complete PFOS removal was achieved within 8 h when the NOM concentration was below 50 mg L-1 as TOC (Supplementary Fig. 17). Notably, the light transmittance (i.e., visual clarity) of the NOM-spiked catholyte increased significantly during PER treatment, likely due to the accelerated transformation of NOM by continuously generated energetic electrons, in addition to direct photolysis. These results highlight the system’s robust performance in the presence of light-absorbing matrices.

The presence of NO3- (10-100 mg L-1) compromised the PFOS treatment (Supplementary Fig. 18) due to the reaction with e-aq. However, since e-aq was continuously produced and NO3- is highly susceptible to both e-aq and electrochemical reduction, the PFOS removal performance should fully recover once NO3- is depleted in a batch operation. The PER process was tested in the presence of CaCl2 (50-150 mg L-1). PFOS removal remained unaffected by Ca2+ (Supplementary Fig. 19). Lastly, the robustness of Pd-TiO2 was demonstrated by its consistent PFOS removal performance, with endpoint efficiencies ranging from 94-98% and first-order rate constants between 0.35-0.42 h-1, remaining stable over five consecutive 8-hour batch operations spanning a total of 40 hours (Supplementary Fig. 20).

All the above results were obtained using a dual-chamber reactor. This design aims to exclude interference from anodic reactions. However, for scale-up, we envision a membrane-less single-chamber configuration as a more practical approach, as it features a simpler reactor configuration and avoids the use of costly ion-exchange membranes. Motivated by the observation that the PER reaction is resistant to dissolved oxygen, we hypothesized that PER can still proceed alongside the anodic water oxidation reaction in a single-chamber reactor.

Further, to maximize UV irradiation efficiency, we propose a tube cathode sheath that encases a UV lamp (Fig. 5a). Before finalizing this concept, we first demonstrated that the placement of the UV lamp, whether positioned between (UV_Mid) or outside (UV_Side) the anode and cathode, does not significantly impact PFOS removal kinetics (Fig. 5b). Based on these findings, we proposed the "UV-in-tube" configuration, which is analogous to the "UV_side" configuration. Another control test was conducted in a single-chamber reactor using a bare titanium tube without a Pd-TiO2 coating under UV lamp irradiation, coupled with an Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox anode (which remained in plate-type as purchased). The results showed no PFOS removal (Supplementary Fig. 21), ruling out adsorption by the Ti substrate and PFOS destruction by the Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox anode via EO. When a tube-type Pd-TiO2 cathode was used, effective PFOS removal (Fig. 5b) and defluorination (DeF = ~40% after PER, Supplementary Fig. 22) were observed. The inner tube surface subjected to both cathodic potential and UV light contributed predominantly to PFAS removal (Supplementary Fig. 23). The full utilization of UV irradiation and the increased electrode area enabled PFOS removal kinetics that were significantly faster than those in the dual-chamber design with a plate-type electrode. Another benefit of a single-chamber reactor is maintaining the pH between 6 and 7 throughout the reaction, thereby avoiding catholyte acidification in the dual-chamber reactor.

During PER treatment using a tubular Pd-TiO2 cathode in the presence of Cl⁻ (1 mM), no negative impact of Cl⁻ on PFOS removal or defluorination was observed (Fig. 5b). Furthermore, free chlorine (< 0.5 mg L-1 detection limit), ClO3- (< 5 μg L-1 detection limit), and ClO4- (< 5 μg L-1 detection limit) were not detected. These results suggest that even if chlorine was formed due to anodic oxidation, it was readily reduced by the Pd-TiO2 cathode alongside PFOS reductive destruction.

To facilitate system scale-up, the Ti tube substrate was replaced with a Ti mesh, which can be more readily fabricated into various geometries and offers greater flexibility in adjusting the available electrode area. We then constructed a mesoscale reactor (Fig. 6a), which is composed of a 16-W low-pressure Hg lamp wrapped by a Pd-TiO2 mesh cathode (256 cm2) and an Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox anode (196 cm2). The mesh Pd-TiO2 enables equally efficient removal of PFOS compared with the tube cathode, benchmarked by specific charge (Ah L-1; Supplementary Fig. 24). The specific energy consumption per order of PFOS removal (SEC) in the lab-prepared electrolyte was calculated as 178 Wh L-1, representing the lowest value reported to date for a PER-based system (Supplementary Table 1). Since the energy consumption of UV (68 Wh L-1) accounted for 38% of the energy consumption, it is reasonable to believe that, should a more energy-efficient UV source (e.g., LED UV) be adopted, the energy consumption could be further reduced.

The mesoscale reactor was applied for the treatment of reverse osmosis membrane concentrate (ROC) derived from the reclamation of municipal wastewater. The ROC contained redox-active anions such as 1950 mg L-1 of Cl- and 37 mg L-1 of NO3-, and background organics at a TOC of 50 mg L-1 (full list of composition see Supplementary Table 6). The ROC was treated as received without adjustment of pH (8.4) or conductivity (8.1 mS cm-1). As demonstrated in Fig. 6b, fluorotelomer sulfonic acid (FTS), PFSA, and PFCA detected in ROC were readily removed after 6 h of PER treatment.

Previously, we used combustion ion chromatography to quantify total fluorine in water.5,42 However, this method is unsuitable for ROC because its high salt content causes matrix interference during combustion, forming stable fluorides (e.g., CaF2, MgF2) that suppress the fluoride signal to near-background levels.43 Nonetheless, the direct analysis of F- in ROC by IC shows that the PER treatment led to an increase of F- concentration, indicating the substantial defluorination of organofluorine (Fig. 6c). No free chlorine was detected throughout the reaction, and no formation of chlorate and perchlorate was identified (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Table 6). The SEC of each target PFAS ranged from 80 to 150 Wh L-1 (Fig. 6e).

Coupling PER with EO toward complete PFAS mineralization
Recently, we discovered that PFAS subjected to homogeneous e-aq-mediated reduction in the UV/S process forms polyfluorinated intermediates that are more susceptible to EO, enabling complete defluorination in a UV/S-EO tandem process.5 Given the excellent performance of PER on driving electron-mediated PFAS reduction, we hypothesize that PER may serve as a chemical-free alternative to UV/S and be effectively integrated with EO. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 22, the PFOS spiked electrolyte was first treated with PER and then subjected to EO with a boron-doped diamond (BDD) anode. The PER-EO tandem process achieved complete destruction of PFOS and ~100% DeF. The results also imply that organic fluorine intermediates were retained in the aqueous phase after PER treatment rather than being released into the gas phase, as complete defluorination in the subsequent EO step would not have been possible otherwise.

The efficacy and practicality of the PER-EO process were further challenged in the treatment of aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) diluted by tap water, representing firefighting equipment cleaning solutions. This wastewater contains 2 mg L-1 total organofluorine, 40 mg L-1 TOC, 7.4 mg L-1 of NO3-, and μg L-1 level of target PFAS (Supplementary Table 6). The diluted AFFF was treated as is throughout the PER-EO process without chemical addition or conductivity adjustment. The PER using the mesoscale single-chamber reactor with a Pd-TiO2 mesh cathode successfully destroyed most of the FTS, PFSA, and PFCA (Fig. 7a-c). Upon transferring to EO treatment, residual PFAS and precursors were further destroyed to reach 100% DeF (Fig. 7d and Supplementary Fig. 25). Removal of 99% of the TOC was achieved after PER-EO treatment (Supplementary Table 6).

In summary, this study reveals mechanisms of cathodic adsorption and energetic electron-mediated defluorination of PFAS on the Pd-TiO2 cathode within a robust, scalable, and highly efficient PER reaction system. These findings advance the fundamental understanding of heterogeneous catalytic reduction of PFAS, a field that has historically lagged behind EO strategies in both mechanistic insight and treatment efficacy. The PER system functions as a standalone treatment capable of achieving substantial PFAS degradation without generating oxyanion byproducts. Compared to homogeneous advanced reduction processes (e.g., UV/S), the PER process eliminates the need for continuous sulfite dosing and operates effectively across a broad native pH range (3–8, as tested in this study) without the need for pH adjustment, whereas UV/S systems typically require strongly alkaline conditions. If complete mineralization of PFAS in chemically complex or non-potable waste streams is prioritized, the integration of PER with EO enables near-complete defluorination in challenging wastewater matrices at ambient conditions, offering flexibility to address different treatment objectives.

## Methods

Chemicals and Materials
Chemicals used as received include sodium sulfate ( J.T.Baker, ≥98%), sulfuric acid (J.T.Baker, 96.7%), palladium chloride (Sigma-Aldrich, 99%), titanium butoxide (Ti(OBu)4, Sigma-Aldrich, 99%), sodium perchlorate monohydrate (Thermal Fisher, 98%), citric acid (Alfa Aesar, 99%), ethylene glycol (Sigma Aldrich, 99%), cadmium perchlorate (Sigma Aldrich, 97%), sodium selenate (Sigma Aldrich, 95%), Heptadecafluorooctanesulfonic acid potassium salt (PFOS, Sigma Aldrich, 98%). ROC samples generated from RO filtration of municipal wastewater were provided by Trussell Tech. The AFFF product diluted by tap water is Platinum Plus C6 3% AFFF Buckeye MIL-SPEC. The Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox anode was purchased from Entrustech, China.

Preparation of Cathode
Titanium (Ti) plates (Grade 2 Titanium sheet, McMaster-Carr, 2.5 cm × 3.2 cm) were polished prior to use. The metal oxide coatings on the Ti plate were deposited by dip-coating in sol-gel precursor solutions followed by calcination. To prepare the coating solutions, we initially prepared a sol-gel by combining 11.5 mg of citric acid with 15.6 ml of ethylene glycol and mixing for 30 min at 60 °C. Subsequently, 0.3 mL of Ti(OBu)4 was added to 5 ml of ethanol, which was then mixed at room temperature. Subsequently, 35 mg PdCl2 and Ti(OBu)4 mixture were added to the sol-gel and mixed for 1 hour at 90 °C. Finally, dilute the coating solution to 50 ml with ethylene glycol. The precursor solution contained 20 mM Ti(OBu)4 and 4 mM PdCl2. The Ti plate was dipped in the coating solution for 20 s, dried at room temperature, and calcinated at 550 °C for 10 min. This cycle was repeated ten times, after which the plate was calcinated at 550 °C for 2 h. The Pd loading amount was adjusted by altering the ratio of Pd to TiO2 in the coating solutions. The coating of Pd-TiO2 on the Ti tube (Grade 9 Titanium tube; Ø 0.55") and mesh (Grade 2 100 mesh opening) follows the same protocol.

Characterization of Cathode
To characterize the catalyst coating without interference from the Ti metal substrate, the catalyst powders were collected by scraping them off the electrode. The powder XRD spectra were recorded with a Bruker instrument (2° to 40°, step 0.5° at 5.0 s per step) using Mo Kα1. SEM imaging was conducted using a JEOL JSM 7600 FEG-SEM with an EDX module. STEM images were performed using a Cs-Corrected Jeol 2100FC Microscopy operating at 200 kV. XPS was measured using a PHI VersaProbe III X-ray Photoelectron Spectrometer (Physical Electronics, USA) equipped with a monochromatic 1486.7 eV Al Kα X-ray source.

PFAS Treatment
The dual-chamber cell configuration was first used to investigate the ER and PER reaction without the interference of the anodic reaction. All electrode areas reported in the manuscript refer to the double-sided projected area submerged in the electrolyte. The Pd-TiO2 cathode (16 cm2) was placed in the cathodic chamber, which contained 100 mL of Na2SO4 catholyte spiked with PFOS (10 µM). An Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox anode (16 cm²) served as the counter electrode. The anolyte was 100 mL of 100 mM H2SO4. To introduce UV254 nm irradiation, a quartz jacketed mini low-pressure Hg lamp (18 W; 5 cm (L) × 0.7 cm (D); Pen-Ray Analytik Jena) was inserted into the catholyte, positioned 0.5 cm from the plate-type cathode.

The scaled-up single-chamber reactor configuration used a tube-type Pd-TiO2 cathode (48 cm2) and a mesh-type Pd-TiO2 cathode (256 cm²). The tube and mesh cathodes were paired with Ir0.3Ta0.7Ox anodes with surface areas of 16 cm2 and 196 cm2, respectively. The tube-type cathode was wrapped around a mini low-pressure Hg lamp (18 W; 5 cm (L) × 0.7 cm (D); Pen-Ray Analytik Jena), while the mesh-type cathode was wrapped around a larger low-pressure Hg lamp (16 W; 26 cm (L) × 1.2 cm (D)).

In the final section of the manuscript, we demonstrate a PER-EO tandem treatment process designed to illustrate a scalable workflow. This approach utilizes an EO flow cell to treat 0.7 L of diluted AFFF following mesoscale PER treatment using a mesh-type Pd-TiO2 cathode. The EO flow reactor, provided by Element Six, is equipped with two BDD disks (4.4 cm in diameter, 0.8 cm inter-electrode spacing) serving as the anode and cathode. The internal volume of the flow cell chamber is 95 mL. During EO treatment, the 0.7 L of PER-treated AFFF was circulated through the cell at a flow rate of 100 mL min-1 under a current of 5 A. The current and flow rate parameters were adopted from our previous study,5 where they were optimized for PFAS degradation, and are applied without modification in this work.

Analysis
Targeted analysis of PFAS was conducted on ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC, Thermo Vanquish) coupled to a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (QQQ MS/MS, Thermo Altis). The analytical method includes 30 PFAS (Table S5). A 10 μL aliquot of the sample was injected and separated on a Thermo Scientific Hypersil GOLD PFP column (2.1 mm × 100 mm, 1.9 μm), maintained at 40 °C. Chromatographic separation utilized a mobile phase A of 5 mM ammonium acetate in water and a mobile phase B of acetonitrile, flowing at a 0.4 mL min-1 rate. The LC gradient was programmed as follows: 0 min (20% B), 0.5 min (20% B), 3 min (80% B), 5 min (100% B), 5.5 min (100% B), 5.6 min (20% B), and 8 min (20% B). The MS parameters were optimized based on selected reaction monitoring (SRM) transitions (precursor/product fragment ion pair). Sample acquisition was conducted using Thermo XCalibur 4.5 software, and subsequent data analysis employed Thermo TraceFinder 5.1 software.

Suspect screening of PFAS TPs was conducted using high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (HPLC/QToF-MS, SCIEX). For the HPLC separation, a 50 μL sample was injected onto a Phenomenex Gemini column (3 μm particle size, 100 × 3 mm) and eluted with ultrapure water (A) and methanol (B), both containing 5 mM ammonium acetate, at a flow rate of 0.6 mL min-1. The gradient was as follows: 90% A-10% B from 0−1.5 minutes, 35% A-65% B from 1.5−8 minutes, 5% A-95% B from 8−8.1 minutes, 1% A-99% B from 8.1−12.5 minutes, and 90% A-10% B from 12.5−15.5 minutes. Data acquisition was turned off for the first 3 min of the run to prevent salts from entering the detector. High-resolution mass spectrometry analysis was performed on a SCIEX X500 QToF mass spectrometer in dual electrospray ionization (ESI) negative mode. A SWATH acquisition method was used in LC-QToF-MS analysis in negative ion mode with ion spray voltage at −4500 V. The QToF-MS/MS was set to scan fragment ions (ranging from 50-2500 Da) for parent ion masses between 100-2500 Da. The validation of polyfluorinated TPs and precursors is based on the following criteria: (i) mass tolerance < 5 ppm; (ii) peak area > 102; (iii) peak area increased with time from time zero.

The analysis of anions (F-, NO3-, SO42-, Cl-, ClO3-, and ClO4-) was performed on a Dionex Aquion ion chromatography system equipped with an anion-exchange column (Thermo Fisher Scientific, RFIC IonPac AS18). The AS18 column operated with a 35 mM KOH solution as the eluent at a flow rate of 1 mL min-1, with a suppressor current set to 57 mA.

ATR-FTIR and in situ FTIR Measurement
The ATR–FTIR measurements were conducted using a Bruker INVENIO-R FTIR spectrometer equipped with a room temperature Deuterated Lanthanum α Alanine doped TriGlycine Sulphate (RT-DLaTGS) detector. A platinum attenuated total reflectance (ATR) accessory with a diamond crystal window was used to collect the FTIR spectra of samples. The scanner velocity is set to 10 kHz. The transmittance spectra ranged from 4,000 to 400 cm−1 and were recorded by averaging 16 scans at a resolution of 4 cm−1.

The operando FTIR experiments were conducted on a Bruker INVENIO-R FTIR spectrometer equipped with an A530/IP electrochemical cell using a liquid nitrogen-cooled mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) detector.

Theoretical Calculation
DFT calculations of the PFOS degradation mechanism on Pd/TiO2 were performed with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Program (VASP; version 6.4) software1,2 using the PBE functional. Wave functions were composed of a summation of plane waves with kinetic energies up to 500 eV. A gamma-point-centered 4×4×1 k-point mesh samples the Brillouin Zone. Electronic structures and energy converged, and energy changes were below 2×10-3 eV when the cut-off energy and k-point mesh were increased to 4×4×1. DFT-D3 corrections based on Grimme et al.3 were used to calculate the nonlocal van der Waals interaction. PAW pseudopotentials reduced the explicitly calculated electrons to the 1s of H; 2s and 2p of O and F, 3s and 3p of S; 3d,3s, and 4p of Ti; 4d,5s, and 5p of Pd. A Hubbard correction of 3.5 eV was placed on the 4d electrons of Ti, following previous studies 6. The Pd [111] and anatase TiO2 [101] facets were used to model the Pd and TiO2 surface, as the XRD results demonstrate that these were the most prevalent in the synthesized materials. The supercells contained 6 × 6 × 5 primitive cell slabs that were separated by at least 15 Å of vacuum space. The middle layer of the Pd slab was frozen, while the entire TiO2 slab was allowed to relax. Atomic geometries of the slabs and PFOS were relaxed until atomic energies changed by less than 0.001 eV. Electronic charge density was calculated using Bader charge analysis7. The solvation effects were included via implicit H2O solvation using VASPsol.44

The pH effects on the adsorption/desorption and surface reaction energies were included using a thermodynamic Hess cycle (Supplementary Fig. 26). The effect of potential on the Pd surface was implemented by means of the computational hydrogen electrode formalism45 and is referenced to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). This approach calculates the reaction free energy at potential U using equation 2:
ΔGprotonation = G0-2.303kT(pKa-pH) (1)
ΔG(U) = ΔG(U0)-ne(U-U0) (2)
where the reaction free energy at 0 V (G(U0)) shifts linearly with potential by -eU (e is the electron charge). Free energies do not include calculated entropies, but rather, only include the entropic contributions due to the potential, entropy of the gas phase molecules as derived from the Hess cycle, and pH effects. Coordinates of all optimized PFAS structures used in the DFT calculations are provided in Supplementary Data 1.
